parts:
Hello everyone,

I have to apologize ahead of time that I am still very much a beginner at graphical models, bayesian statistics, and obviously Stan. My problem is that I have a Stan model that's taking forever to fit. It's basically taking a full working day for it to run through 3 chains of 1000 iterations. It might just the fact that for this data for this model, that's how long it takes, but I'd appreciate any advice on optimizing the model.

I've attached my data as an R workspace. The response variable is F1.n, which is an acoustic measurement of a specific vowel. I have observations from 308 speakers, who spoke this vowel in 429 different words. I am interested in the rate of change of F1.n in two different linguistic contexts over dates of birth. Here's what a basic plot of speaker means looks like.






















I'm specifically interested in whether the rates of change are ever the same between NContext==1 and NContext==2, i.e. are they ever parallel? In this case it seems obvious that they aren't, but I'll be looking at other cases where this isn't so obvious. Also, in this case, men and women look to be basically the same, there are other cases I'll look at where they're definitely not.

I've decided to model the rate of change using b-splines, because I understand how to implement them. So, I have a parameter in the model delta[i], which represents the amount of change from DOB==-i-1 to DOB==1, which is modeled with a b-spline. I also have a parameter Delta[i], which is equal to sum(delta[1:i]), which represents the total displacement from DOB==1. Here's my Stan model.

model_code <- "
data{
  int<lower = 0> N;           // number of observations
  real y[N];                  // y
  int<lower = 0> speaker[N];  // speaker index
  int<lower = 0> word[N];     // word index

  int<lower = 0> context[N];  // context index
  int<lower = 0> max_context; // max context

  int<lower = 0> max_speaker;      // number of speakers
  int<lower = 0> dob[max_speaker]; // by speaker dob
  int<lower = 0> sex[max_speaker]; // by speaker sex
  int<lower = 0> max_sex;          // max sex
  int<lower = 0> n_bspline;        // number of b-spline knots
  int<lower = 0> max_dob;          // max_dob
 
  matrix[max_dob, n_bspline] b_spline;   // bsplines
  int<lower = 0> max_word;        // max word
}
parameters{
  vector[n_bspline] b_coefs;           // bspline coefs for sex==1, context==1
  vector[n_bspline] male_b_coefs;      // bspline coefs for sex==2, context==1
  vector[n_bspline] c2_b_coefs;        // bspline coefs for sex==1, context==2
  vector[n_bspline] c2_male_b_coefs;   // bspline coefs for sex==2, context==2


  matrix[max_speaker, max_context] speaker_mu;   // by-speaker mu
  real<lower = 0> speaker_sigma[max_speaker];    // by-speaker sigma

  real<lower = 0> sigma;              // sigma for distribution of speaker_mu
  real intercept;                    // intercept for speaker_mu
  real male_effect;                   // male effect for speaker_mu
  real context_effect;                // context effect for speaker_mu

  real word_mu[max_word];            // by-word mu
  real<lower = 0> words_sigma;       // sigma for distribution of word_mu
}
transformed parameters{
  // delta[i] = diff in y from dob==i-1 to dob==i
  vector[max_dob] delta;           // delta for for sex==1, context==1     
  vector[max_dob] male_delta;      // delta for for sex==2, context==1
  vector[max_dob] c2_delta;        // delta for for sex==1, context==2
  vector[max_dob] c2_male_delta;   // delta for for sex==2, context==2

  // Delta = total displacement from dob==1
  real Delta[max_dob, max_sex, max_context]; 

  // mu for intercept prior
  real likely_start;

  // calculate deltas
  delta <- b_spline * b_coefs;
  male_delta <- b_spline * male_b_coefs;

  c2_delta <- b_spline * c2_b_coefs;
  c2_male_delta <- b_spline * c2_male_b_coefs;


  // This whole block is basicaly cumsum(delta[1:i])
  Delta[1,1,1] <- delta[1];
  Delta[1,1,2] <- delta[1] + c2_delta[1];
  Delta[1,2,1] <- delta[1] + male_delta[1];
  Delta[1,2,2] <- delta[1] + c2_delta[1] + male_delta[1] + c2_male_delta[1];

  for(i in 2:max_dob){
    Delta[i,1,1] <- Delta[i-1,1,1] + delta[i];
    Delta[i,1,2] <- Delta[i-1,1,2] + delta[i] + c2_delta[i];
    Delta[i,2,1] <- Delta[i-1,2,1] + delta[i] + male_delta[i];
    Delta[i,2,2] <- Delta[i-1,2,2] + delta[i] + c2_delta[i] + male_delta[i] + c2_male_delta[i];
  }
  //end cumsum

  // Set mu for intercept prior to sample mean
likely_start <- mean(y);
}
model{

  // sigma prior as suggested by Stan reference
  words_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5) T[0,];  // sigma for distribution of word effects
  for(i in 1:max_word){
     word_mu[i] ~ normal(0, words_sigma);  // word effect
   }
  // Calculate a mu for every speaker for each context
  for(i in 1:max_speaker){
    for(j in 1:max_context){
      speaker_mu[i,j] ~ normal(Delta[dob[i],sex[i],j] + (male_effect * (sex[i]-1)) + (context_effect * (j-1)) + intercept, sigma);
    }
    // Each speaker can have a different sigma for their data.
    speaker_sigma[i] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5) T[0,];
  }

  // priors for parameters in speaker_mu estimate
  intercept ~ normal(likely_start, 100);
  male_effect ~ normal(0, 100);
  context_effect ~ normal(0,100);
  // b_coefs
  for(i in 1:n_bspline){
    b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    male_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    c2_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    c2_male_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
  }

  // data loop
  // mu = speaker_mu + word_mu
  // sigma = speaker_sigma
  for(i in 1:N){
    y[i] ~ normal(speaker_mu[speaker[i], context[i]] + word_mu[word[i]], speaker_sigma[speaker[i]]);
  }
}

Hi Josef,

There are a number of things you can do to speed things up with your model.  One big thing you can do is use the vectorized form of the normal distribution.

E.G.,  instead of

for(i in 1:max_word){
     word_mu[i] ~ normal(0, words_sigma);  // word effect

}

and

  // b_coefs

for(i in 1:n_bspline){
    b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    male_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    c2_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
    c2_male_b_coefs[i] ~ normal(0, 100);
  }

you can simply write

word_mu ~ normal(0,words_sigma);
b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);
male_b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);
c2_b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);
c2_male_b_coefs ~ normal(0,100);

which should be a fair bit faster.

Your cumsum would probably be faster done as follows:

Instead of

// This whole block is basicaly cumsum(delta[1:i])
  Delta[1,1,1] <- delta[1];
  Delta[1,1,2] <- delta[1] + c2_delta[1];
  Delta[1,2,1] <- delta[1] + male_delta[1];
  Delta[1,2,2] <- delta[1] + c2_delta[1] + male_delta[1] + c2_male_delta[1];

  for(i in 2:max_dob){
    Delta[i,1,1] <- Delta[i-1,1,1] + delta[i];
    Delta[i,1,2] <- Delta[i-1,1,2] + delta[i] + c2_delta[i];
    Delta[i,2,1] <- Delta[i-1,2,1] + delta[i] + male_delta[i];
    Delta[i,2,2] <- Delta[i-1,2,2] + delta[i] + c2_delta[i] + male_delta[i] + c2_male_delta[i];
  }
  //end cumsum

Use

  for(i in 1:max_dob){
    t0 <- sum(delta[1:i]);
    t1 <- sum(c2_delta[1:i]);
    t2 <- sum(male_delta[1:i]);
    Delta[i,1,1] <- t0
    Delta[i,1,2] <- t0 + t1;
    Delta[i,2,1] <- t0 + t2;
    Delta[i,2,2] <- Delta[i,1,2] + t2 + sum(c2_male_delta[1:i]);
  }

There may be a few others that can be done now but that's a start.  Right now indexing limitations will prevent making other big gains (e.g., vectorizing y or speaker_mu) but become available in the future.

Hope this helps.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: reading RStan models from files vs. strings
parts:
I strongly recommend using the

file=<filepath>

argument to stan() in RStan to specify a model
from a file rather than the

model_code=<string>

argument to specify the model as a string.

Whatever you do, don't cut and paste from a file
into a string. Not only is it tedious, it's
error prone (c.f., Fitts's law).

I think people may not realize the file option is
there because the first example in the RStan getting
started guide uses a string rather than a file, as does
the example in the draft appendix of the 3rd edition
of BDA.

- Bob

Ah. My motivation was to cut down cut-and-paste errors.
If you have an entire R script in a file along with
the model, that arrangement makes sense, too.

I tend to run models with different data, though, and
like to keep the following concerns separated:

-- model
-- R code (or other code) to munge data
-- R code to call fit code (including inits)
-- R code to draw plots and analyze
-- one script to run everything for an analysis

The main reason is that I often run the same model over
data from different sources with different shapes and then
run different output analyses over them.

The style in R is to have one big function do everything,
which gives you nice encapsulation but lower flexibility,
whereas my arrangement is more unix-like, which is more
modular, but less encapsulated.

I was only looking for where the error in parsing/compiling
came from.

You can get a whole lot more efficiency by vectorizing
the call to

speaker_mu[i,j] ~ normal(...);

Allocate a vector for the means, fill it with the mean
values in a loop, then call vectorized normal all at
once. That means replacing this:

for (i in 1:max_speaker) {
for (j in 1:max_context) {

speaker_mu[i,j] ~ normal(Delta[dob[i],sex[i],j]
+ (male_effect * (sex[i]-1))
+ (context_effect * (j-1))
+ intercept,
sigma);
}
speaker_sigma[i] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5) T[0,];
}

with this:


for (i in 1:max_speaker) {
real predix[max_context];
for (j in 1:max_context)
predix[j] <- Delta[dob[i],sex[i],j]

+ (male_effect * (sex[i]-1))
+ (context_effect * (j-1))

+ intercept;
speaker_mu[i] ~ normal(predix,sigma);
}

for (i in 1:I)
speaker_sigma[i] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

Note you don't need truncation because sigma's constrained
to (0,inf) and we only need computation to a proportion (and
those cumulatives are expensive!).

You could also put it all in one big array, which is even
faster, but requires loop fiddling. We'll eventually get around
to vectorizing to matrices, but we're doing vectors for
everything first.

And then the same trick with N, which is even more important
if N is large relative to everything else:

}

real spkr_sigma_spkr[N];

spkr_sigma_spkr[i] <- speaker_sigma[speaker[i]]);

function used in an assignment.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Can I optimize my complex, and slow to fit model?
parts:
On 9/21/12 4:44 PM, Josef Fruehwald wrote:
> Just so I understand the basics, this is what I understand from your advice:
>
> 1) I won't be eliminating any loops, but will be changing what's done inside of a loop.
> 2) It's less expensive to create a vector and assign values into it through a loop and then do the vectorized sampling,
> than it is to do the sampling inside of the loop.
>
> Is that right?

Right.

It's not the loops that are expensive, it's the sampling
statements executed inside them. Assignments and vector
allocations (implied by local variable declarations) are
relatively inexpensive (probably not even measurable as
a fraction of total work in cases like yours).

For reasons having to do with how automatic differentation
of the log probability function is done, it's MUCH MUCH
more efficient to call one vectorized sampling statement than
to call the individual sampling statements in a loop.
It saves substantial work in allocation, reduces memory
usage, and greatly reduces the number of virtual function
calls (the big bottleneck for modern CPUs is figuring
out where a program will branch to and a bunch of
very unpredictable virtual function calls is about as bad
as it gets for that).

For what it's worth, you can open the hood on JAGS and
add vectorized distributions there. This provides a pretty
big speedup for similar reasons (they interpret loops and
function calls -- we interpret expressions during auto-dif).

- Bob
